implementation_notes: futures is where the composite starts in async Rust: stream::iter(parts).map(route) builds one future per part, buffer_unordered(n) runs up to n of them concurrently and yields results as they finish (buffered(n) preserves input order), and collect()/fold() performs the aggregation - the concurrency limit is explicit, which the classic form usually lacks. Ownership is the correlation state: each future owns its part and the collected Vec is the merge input, so no shared mutable aggregator is required. Use the ordered form whenever the merge is not commutative.
pitfalls: buffer_unordered loses input order; use buffered(n) or carry the part index when the aggregate depends on order.
Closures that borrow the composite message will not be Send for tokio::spawn - take ownership of each part or use scoped tasks, or the composite does not compile.
futures::future::join_all builds every future eagerly with no bound; for large part counts prefer buffer_unordered/for_each_concurrent.

variants.name: Rayon parallel iterator (CPU-bound parts)
variants.implementation_notes: Rayon turns the split into data-parallel iteration: par_iter().map(route) distributes the parts over the thread pool and reduce (or fold/collect) merges them, so the aggregation is written as a genuine divide-and-conquer reduction with an identity and an associative combine - exactly the shape the trait documents. Use it for CPU-bound parts, keep futures for async I/O, and do not block an async runtime's worker threads with rayon work.
pitfalls: reduce requires an associative combine with a true identity (the docs state this); a non-associative merge gives non-deterministic aggregates.
Rayon's global pool is shared with the rest of the program: blocking or nested parallelism inside a part can starve it - use a scoped ThreadPool for isolation.
A panic in any part unwinds through the reduce and loses the partial aggregate; panic_fuse or catch_unwind is needed for partial results.
